query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in HEAs promotes a self-organizing redistribution of elements during high-temperature exposure, selectively enriching protective oxide-formers (e.g., Cr and/or Al) at the metal surface. This local enrichment drives the nucleation and growth of a dense, adherent oxide layer (e.g., chromia and/or alumina) that resists further oxidation, while suppressing the formation of less-protective oxides (e.g., Mn-oxides).
generation.material_initial_state: An as-manufactured, homogeneous high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi or an AlTiNiCuCox variant) with a uniform distribution of its constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to high-temperature oxidation conditions (>800 °C) under systematically varied oxygen partial pressures and through well-defined thermal cycles, while performing real-time in situ X-ray and photoelectron spectroscopy.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (above 800 °C) in environments ranging from low oxygen partial pressures (vacuum-like conditions) to ambient air, including thermal cycling to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a compositional gradient at the oxide/metal interface where protective elements (Cr and/or Al) become locally enriched due to rapid, entropy-driven diffusion, while non-protective elements (e.g., Mn) remain depleted in the scale formation zone.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy enables rapid, local elemental diffusion and segregation under oxidative stress. This synergistic effect favors the formation of thermodynamically stable and kinetically sluggish-growing protective oxides (such as Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3) that form a continuous, adherent layer. This layer acts as a barrier, preventing further oxygen ingress and further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Real-time in situ measurements will show an early-stage, localized enrichment of protective elements at the surface, followed by the formation of a thin, uniform, and adherent protective oxide layer that grows slowly over time. In contrast, a conventional alloy or HEA lacking these synergistic benefits will display more rapid growth of less-uniform, non-protective oxide scales characterized by the formation of Mn-rich oxides and evidence of scale spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: A conventional alloy or an HEA composition in which the balance of oxide-forming elements does not support self-organized enrichment (leading to less selective, non-protective oxide formation under identical high-temperature oxidation conditions).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate at elevated temperatures (>800 °C) under oxygen partial pressures from near-vacuum to ambient air. Variations in alloy composition, particularly the relative amounts of Cr, Al, and Mn, as well as differences in thermal cycling profiles, may influence the protective behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact contributions and relative importance of individual elements (e.g., Cr versus Al) in driving the protective behavior remain uncertain, as does the quantitative scale of the effect. Outcomes may also vary with minor changes in alloy composition or environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform high-temperature in situ oxidation experiments on the target HEA and a conventional alloy control under identical conditions (using varying oxygen partial pressures and thermal cycling). Use real-time X-ray and XPS analyses to track elemental redistribution and oxide phase formation at the metal/oxide interface.
measurements: Elemental concentration profiles (via XPS/EDS) at the interface over time
Phase identification and thickness measurements of the formed oxide layer (via in situ XRD and TEM)
Assessment of oxide scale uniformity and adherence (via in situ microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ analyses fail to detect a selective, consistent enrichment of protective elements (e.g., Cr or Al) at the oxidation front in the HEA, or if the oxide layers formed are similar in composition, structure, and adherence to those on the conventional alloy (e.g., dominated by non-protective Mn-oxides with evident spallation), then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy drives synergistic formation of a protective oxide layer is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. In this work, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA was successfully fabricated through the arc-melting process, with an emphasis on phase, microstructure, and real-time oxidation behaviour in two different non-ambient (high-temperature and low-oxygen partial pressure) conditions. The main findings of this research work can be summarised as follows. In a vacuum (4.2 × 10−6 atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation, contrary to ThermoCalc’s prediction of both halite and spinel oxides, and Ni/Co forming halite. In air (1.0 atm), vigorous oxidation was observed, with most of the oxides formed being spinel. Mn remained important in the formation of spinel oxides, and Co was predicted to form spinel oxides by ThermoCalc but was not found in oxide-forming elements. Oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4 were not detected during in situ HTXRD in either vacuum or air, which contrasts with previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. Mn was found to be a higher oxide-forming element, producing non-protective oxides, and leading to the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer. Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 presents line scanning energy spectrum diagrams of the cross section of the AlTiNiCuCo1.0 alloy oxide layer after oxidation for 50 and 100 h at 800 °C. After 100 h oxidation, the oxide film was thicker than that after 50 h, but the change in thickness was not apparent. This indicates that the oxide film of an HEA of this composition under high-temperature oxidation is relatively dense and plays a certain protective role for the alloy; thus, the alloy has better high-temperature oxidation resistance. It can be seen from Figure 8a, representing 50 h oxidation, that the oxide layer still contained large amounts of Al, Ti, and O elements. It was presumed that there were mainly two oxides, Al2O3 and TiO2, in the oxide layer. After oxidation for 100 h, the contents of Al and Ti in the oxide layer were greater, and the content of Co was significantly increased. Combining this with XRD analysis results, it was found that there were three oxides present: CoAl2O4, Al2O3, and TiO2.

decision.trend: From the 2019 study (PMC6513993) showing that a novel refractory HEA can form a stable CrTaO4-based oxide protective layer under long-term high-temperature exposure, there has been increasing interest in how multi-principal elements selectively form protective scales. In another work from 2019 (PMC7515071), wear resistance was closely tied to formation of protective oxides in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5. In 2021 (PMC8468823), it was shown that adjusting individual constituent fractions (e.g., Co content) affects scale density and improves high-temperature oxidation resistance of AlTiNiCuCox. Most recently (PMC11169556), advanced in-situ methods were used to reveal that multi-element interactions and local thermodynamic factors drive the stage-by-stage development of protective surface oxides in HEAs. Despite these insights, the underlying mechanism of how multiple principal elements synergize to form and maintain stable, adherent oxide scales remains only partially understood.
decision.unsolved: It is not yet fully clear how the interplay among different oxide-forming elements at elevated temperatures is kinetically self-regulating. Specifically, the role of high configurational entropy—whether it fosters a self-organizing, stable oxide scale that resists spallation and phase separation—still needs to be conclusively demonstrated and quantified. Additionally, it is unknown if different partial pressures of oxygen or thermal cycling conditions can disrupt this synergy, leading to compromised protective scale formation and oxidation resistance.
decision.lever: Conduct real-time, high-temperature in-situ X-ray and photoelectron spectroscopy under systematically varied oxygen partial pressures and thermal cycles to track transient oxide formation and measure composition profiles at the evolving surface.
decision.why: By observing oxide-scale nucleation and growth as it happens, one can test the hypothesis that the multi-element synergy in HEAs selectively drives certain stable oxide phases to form and remain adherent. The key indicators would be whether localized elemental redistribution establishes a dense, protective layer under higher oxygen pressures and thermal cycling. If this synergy-based mechanism dominates, one would see consistent phase selection and composition profiles in the early stages of oxidation and minimal scale disruption under cycling. If, however, the scale becomes non-protective (e.g., by spallation or the formation of non-protective oxides) when oxidation conditions vary, the synergy hypothesis—and its predicted robust responsiveness to environment—would be falsified.
